title: Joshua 13:15–23
context: This section describes Reuben’s territory east of the Dead Sea, from the Arnon valley north through the plateau around Medeba and Heshbon. Many towns recall earlier events: battles with Sihon, Israel’s sin at Peor, Moses’ view from Pisgah, and the death of Balaam with the Midianite leaders. The list records God’s promise made concrete. Some sites cannot be identified with certainty, and both traditions read the passage as shared ground.

verses.text: Moses gave to the tribe of the children of Reuben according to their families.
verses.arminianNotes:
Moses gave Reuben its inheritance according to its families. The detailed allotment begins.

Arminian readers see each family included in God’s provision. No one is overlooked, and every household has a place to call its own.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase ‘according to their families’ stresses ordered distribution. The land is given household by household.

Reformed readers see God’s care reaching to every clan. Both traditions read this as shared ground, seeing the allotment lists as a record of God’s promise made concrete for real families.

verses.text: Their border was from Aroer, that is on the edge of the valley of the Arnon, and the city that is in the middle of the valley, and all the plain by Medeba;
verses.arminianNotes:
Reuben’s border runs from Aroer on the Arnon and the city in the valley through the plain by Medeba. The southern boundary is repeated.

Arminian readers see clear borders that help prevent disputes between tribes.
verses.reformedNotes:
The description repeats verse 9 for Reuben in particular. Precision matters for inheritance.

Reformed readers see order in how God’s gifts are distributed. Both traditions read this constructively as shared ground, without claiming more certainty about each location than the evidence allows.

verses.text: Heshbon, and all its cities that are in the plain; Dibon, Bamoth Baal, Beth Baal Meon,
verses.arminianNotes:
Heshbon and its cities in the plain, Dibon, Bamoth Baal, and Beth Baal Meon belong to Reuben. Several names contain ‘Baal,’ recalling the region’s earlier worship.

Arminian readers see former centers of other gods becoming part of Israel’s inheritance.
verses.reformedNotes:
The towns are named one by one. Some later came under Moabite control, as Isaiah 15–16 suggests.

Reformed readers see the land given yet still needing to be held faithfully. Both traditions read this list as shared ground.

verses.arminianNotes:
Jahaz, Kedemoth, and Mephaath are listed. Jahaz was where Israel fought Sihon (Numbers 21:23).

Arminian readers see places of past battles becoming places of settled life. Conflict gives way to homes, fields, and families.
verses.reformedNotes:
The list continues with towns in the plateau. Each name records part of God’s gift.

Reformed readers see the steady recording of God’s faithfulness. Both traditions read this as shared ground, and note that Kedemoth and Mephaath later appear, with Jahaz, among the Levitical cities from Reuben in Joshua 21:36–37.

verses.text: Kiriathaim, Sibmah, Zereth Shahar in the mount of the valley,
verses.arminianNotes:
Kiriathaim, Sibmah, and Zereth Shahar ‘in the mount of the valley’ are added. Not all these sites are certainly identified.

Arminian readers see the list as a testimony to real places that Israel received.
verses.reformedNotes:
The names fill out Reuben’s territory. Some are hard to locate today.

Reformed readers see such lists as part of Scripture’s witness to God’s faithfulness in history. Both traditions read this constructively and with appropriate caution about identification.

verses.text: Beth Peor, the slopes of Pisgah, Beth Jeshimoth,
verses.arminianNotes:
Beth Peor, the slopes of Pisgah, and Beth Jeshimoth belong to Reuben. Peor recalls Israel’s sin in Numbers 25, and Pisgah is where Moses viewed the land (Deuteronomy 34:1).

Arminian readers see memories of failure and hope bound up in these places.
verses.reformedNotes:
The places carry strong associations. Moses was buried in the valley opposite Beth Peor (Deuteronomy 34:6).

Reformed readers see God’s story written into the land. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: all the cities of the plain, and all the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon, whom Moses struck with the chiefs of Midian, Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba, the princes of Sihon, who lived in the land.
verses.arminianNotes:
All the plain and Sihon’s kingdom are Reuben’s, with mention of the Midianite chiefs Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba, princes allied with Sihon. Numbers 31:8 names the same five.

Arminian readers see past events recalled to explain the present inheritance.
verses.reformedNotes:
The Midianite leaders are linked with Sihon. The verse joins two earlier accounts.

Reformed readers see the land as the outcome of God’s past acts. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, without speculating beyond what the text says about the alliance.

verses.text: The children of Israel also killed Balaam the son of Beor, the soothsayer, with the sword, among the rest of their slain.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel also killed Balaam son of Beor, the soothsayer, among the slain. The prophet hired to curse Israel died with Israel’s enemies.

Arminian readers see Balaam’s end as the outcome of his choices; Numbers 31:16 links him with the sin at Peor.
verses.reformedNotes:
Balaam is called a soothsayer here, a term for forbidden divination. Numbers 31:8 also records his death.

Reformed readers see God’s justice reaching one who opposed his people. Both traditions read this plainly, and 2 Peter 2:15 and Revelation 2:14 later treat Balaam as a warning.

verses.text: The border of the children of Reuben was the bank of the Jordan. This was the inheritance of the children of Reuben according to their families, the cities and its villages.
verses.arminianNotes:
Reuben’s western border is the Jordan; this is its inheritance with cities and villages. The allotment closes.

Arminian readers see a complete and orderly gift. Reuben has a defined place among the tribes.
verses.reformedNotes:
The summary formula marks the end of Reuben’s section. The same pattern will close each allotment.

Reformed readers see God’s promise fulfilled in measurable terms. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God giving each tribe its portion.
